patient.name: Kenneth Doyle
patient.complaint: Three weeks of worsening confusion and drowsiness that 'comes and goes', after a fall
background: Drinks about 30 units of alcohol a week
Fell in the garden 4 weeks ago and hit his head; seemed fine afterwards
Widower, lives alone in Walthamstow; daughter visits daily

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an elderly, anticoagulated or alcoholic patient who fell, then fluctuating confusion over days to weeks; distractors are dementia, extradural haemorrhage, stroke and tumour.

points: Kenneth, 81, tripped and hit his head **4 weeks ago**.
He seemed fine, so nobody sought help.
Over 3 weeks: headaches, forgetfulness, **two more falls**.
His daughter says some days he is **sharp, others muddled**.
Today he is too drowsy to get out of bed.

steps.lead: Kenneth's minor fall weeks ago could have torn a **bridging vein**: a slow venous bleed between dura and arachnoid that surfaces late.
Kenneth has almost every risk factor: **over 65**, **warfarin**, alcohol (atrophy), and repeated falls.

visual.title: Kenneth's GCS over his first 24 hours
visual.caption: Up and down, trending down: the **fluctuating GCS** of a subdural.

steps.lead: Kenneth's confusion, falls and **fluctuating consciousness** are the classic picture; his mild left arm drift is a focal sign.

steps.q: Which diagnosis best explains Kenneth's picture?
steps.r: Elderly, anticoagulated, a head injury weeks ago and **fluctuating** confusion: **chronic subdural**. Dementia does not fluctuate like this or follow a fall.

steps.lead: Kenneth's CT shows a **crescent** over the right hemisphere crossing the sutures, mostly **hypodense**: a chronic bleed, about 4 weeks old.

steps.text: Do not label an elderly patient with new, **fluctuating** confusion and falls as 'dementia'. Check the anticoagulant history and scan the head.

investigation.exam: Expect non-contrast CT head as the answer, or a CT description to interpret: crescent crossing sutures, and density that changes with age.

steps.q: What is the investigation of choice for Kenneth?
steps.r: **Urgent non-contrast CT head** is the gold standard: fast, available and shows blood.

steps.lead: Kenneth's CT confirms a **crescent-shaped** collection that crosses suture lines, with sulcal effacement and 8 mm midline shift.

visual.title: Subdural density on CT by age of bleed
visual.label: Kenneth 4 weeks
visual.caption: Blood fades from bright to dark as it liquefies. Isodense subacute bleeds are easy to miss.

steps.title: Bloods on arrival
steps.text: Supratherapeutic INR drives expansion; raised MCV fits his alcohol intake. Normal sodium and glucose exclude metabolic mimics.

visual.title: Midline shift on CT
visual.label: Kenneth 8 mm
visual.caption: Shift above 5 mm with symptoms means neurosurgery.

steps.text: **Acute-on-chronic** subdural shows mixed density: bright fresh blood within a darker old collection.
A **lens-shaped** bleed that stops at suture lines is extradural, not subdural. Crescent and crossing sutures = subdural.

management.exam: Expect: reverse anticoagulation (vitamin K + PCC; idarucizumab for dabigatran), burr hole for chronic, craniotomy for acute, observation for small asymptomatic bleeds.

steps.lead: Kenneth is symptomatic and anticoagulated: **reverse the warfarin** and refer to neurosurgery now.
For Kenneth: stop warfarin, **IV vitamin K 5 mg** plus **4-factor PCC**. If he took dabigatran, the answer would be idarucizumab.

steps.q: Kenneth has a symptomatic **chronic** subdural with 8 mm shift. What operation?
steps.r: Liquefied chronic blood drains through a **burr hole**. Craniotomy is first-line for **acute** clotted subdurals.

steps.lead: Kenneth's chronic collection is drained through a **burr hole** once his INR is corrected.

steps.title: Subdural decision pathway
nodes: Symptoms, raised ICP or shift >5 mm?

steps.lead: Had Kenneth's bleed been a small, asymptomatic acute subdural, he would be **observed** with regular neuro checks and **serial CT**.

visual.title: Kenneth after reversal and burr hole
visual.caption: INR corrected within the hour; GCS recovers once the collection is drained.

steps.text: If ICP is high and surgery is not immediately available, **hyperventilation** to hypocapnia buys short-term time only.

steps.lead: NICE NG232 (head injury) says anticoagulated patients with a head injury need a **CT within 8 hours**, even if well.

steps.text: Do not restart Kenneth's warfarin on discharge without a specialist decision: stroke risk from AF versus re-bleed risk.

science.exam: Applied mechanism: bridging veins and atrophy, why venous bleeds are slow, why the crescent crosses sutures, and why reversal is urgent.

steps.lead: Kenneth's alcohol and age have **shrunk his brain**, stretching the bridging veins so a small jolt shears them.

steps.title: Why the elderly bleed
nodes: Bridging veins stretched across a wider gap
Slow venous ooze into subdural space

steps.lead: Venous pressure is low, so Kenneth's bleed grew **slowly**: no symptoms for a week, then gradual decline.
The subdural space is not anchored at sutures, so Kenneth's blood spread over the whole hemisphere: a **crescent**.

steps.q: Why does an extradural haematoma stop at the suture lines?
o: Dura is firmly attached to the skull at the sutures
steps.r: Extradural blood lies **between skull and dura**, and the dura is tethered at sutures, giving a lens shape.

steps.lead: Kenneth's collection became **hypodense** as it liquefied; fragile neomembranes can rebleed and make it grow.
Every hour Kenneth stayed anticoagulated risked **haematoma expansion**; that is why reversal came first.

mcq.q: Which vessels bleed in a subdural haemorrhage?
mcq.r: Torn **bridging veins** between cortex and dural sinuses.

mcq.q: What is the classic conscious level pattern in subdural haemorrhage?
mcq.r: **Fluctuating consciousness**; a lucid interval is extradural.

mcq.q: Which patient is most at risk of chronic subdural?
o: 82 year old on warfarin with falls

mcq.q: What shape is a subdural haemorrhage on CT?
How does a 4-week-old subdural appear on CT?
First-line surgery for a symptomatic chronic subdural?
mcq.r: Liquefied blood drains through a **burr hole**.

mcq.q: Which midline shift on CT indicates surgery for an acute subdural?
mcq.r: **Midline shift >5 mm**, raised ICP or deteriorating neurology.

mcq.q: Why does a subdural present slowly?
mcq.r: **Venous** blood accumulates more slowly than arterial.

glossary.subdural: The space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.
glossary.dura mater: The tough outer layer of the meninges, lining the skull.
glossary.arachnoid mater: The thin middle meningeal layer, beneath the dura.
glossary.bridging veins: Veins crossing the subdural space from the cortex to the dural venous sinuses.
glossary.dural venous sinuses: Venous channels within the dura that drain blood from the brain.
glossary.extradural: Between the skull and the dura; bleeds are usually from the middle meningeal artery.
glossary.extradural haemorrhage: Arterial bleed between skull and dura with a lucid interval and a lens-shaped CT appearance.
glossary.middle meningeal artery: Artery under the temple whose rupture causes most extradural haematomas.
glossary.lucid interval: A period of recovered consciousness between injury and deterioration, classic of extradural bleeds.
glossary.fluctuating consciousness: Conscious level that varies over hours to days, classic of subdural haemorrhage.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, scoring eye, verbal and motor response from 3 to 15.
glossary.crescent-shaped: Curved like a new moon, hugging the brain surface: the subdural CT shape.
glossary.biconvex: Lens-shaped, bulging both ways: the extradural CT shape.
glossary.suture lines: The joints between skull bones, where the dura is firmly attached.
glossary.extra-axial: Outside the brain tissue itself but inside the skull.
glossary.sulcal effacement: Loss of visible sulci on CT from brain compression.
glossary.midline shift: Displacement of midline brain structures by a mass; over 5 mm favours surgery.
glossary.hyperdense: Brighter than brain on CT, as with fresh blood.
glossary.isodense: The same density as brain on CT, as with a subacute subdural.
glossary.hypodense: Darker than brain on CT, as with a chronic, liquefied subdural.
glossary.acute-on-chronic: Fresh bleeding into an existing chronic collection, giving mixed density on CT.
glossary.neomembrane: New fibrous membrane forming around a chronic subdural, with fragile vessels that rebleed.
glossary.liquefaction: Breakdown of clot into fluid over weeks.
glossary.brain atrophy: Shrinkage of brain tissue with age or alcohol, stretching bridging veins.
glossary.coagulopathy: Impaired blood clotting from disease or drugs.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio, measuring warfarin effect; high means more bleeding risk.
glossary.craniotomy: Removing a bone flap to evacuate clot, then replacing it.
glossary.burr hole craniostomy: Drilling a small hole in the skull to drain liquefied chronic subdural blood.
glossary.decompressive craniectomy: Removing part of the skull and leaving it off to relieve pressure.
glossary.hyperventilation: Over-breathing to lower CO2, constricting cerebral vessels and briefly reducing ICP.
glossary.PCC: Prothrombin complex concentrate, replacing factors II, VII, IX and X to reverse warfarin fast.
glossary.4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate: Concentrate of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X for urgent warfarin reversal.
glossary.vitamin K: Restores warfarin-blocked clotting factor synthesis; given IV in a bleed.
glossary.serial CT: Repeated CT scans to watch whether a bleed grows.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume; raised by alcohol excess and B12 or folate deficiency.
glossary.herniation: Displacement of brain tissue through a rigid opening from raised pressure.

technique.stem: An 84 year old woman has been increasingly confused and drowsy for 2 weeks. Her son says some days she is her normal self. She fell and hit her head a month ago. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 152/84 mmHg. Her GCS is 13. She has a mild right pronator drift.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis in an elderly, confused patient.

clues: some days she is her normal self
fell and hit her head a month ago
steps.x: Elderly, anticoagulated, fall weeks ago, fluctuating confusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic subdural haemorrhage.**

elim: Gradual over years, without fluctuation or a recent fall.
Rapid deterioration after a lucid interval of hours.
Sudden onset, not 2 weeks of fluctuation.

steps.x: **B. Chronic subdural haemorrhage.** Elderly + anticoagulant + fall + fluctuating confusion = chronic subdural.

technique.stem: A 77 year old man who drinks heavily is brought in after several falls this week. He is drowsy with a headache. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 164/90 mmHg. His GCS is 12 and fluctuating. Capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation.
Alcohol, falls, fluctuating GCS, hypoglycaemia excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent non-contrast CT head.**

elim: Dangerous with a possible mass lesion and raised ICP.
Slower and less available; CT is gold standard.

steps.x: **E. Non-contrast CT head.** Suspected intracranial bleed = non-contrast CT.

technique.stem: A 34 year old man is hit on the head during a fight. He arrives with a GCS of 10. His pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 168/92 mmHg. CT head shows a hyperdense crescent-shaped collection over the left hemisphere crossing the suture lines with 9 mm midline shift. He takes no anticoagulants.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management of an acute subdural.
Acute subdural, shift >5 mm, low GCS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Craniotomy with clot evacuation.**

elim: For liquefied chronic subdurals; acute clot will not drain.

steps.x: **B. Craniotomy with clot evacuation.** Acute + shift >5 mm = craniotomy; chronic = burr hole.

technique.stem: A 79 year old man fell 3 weeks ago. He was well for the first week, then developed gradually worsening headache and confusion. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/80 mmHg. CT shows a subdural haemorrhage.
technique.q: Which best explains the delay between injury and symptoms?
o: CSF leak through a dural tear
Slow accumulation of low-pressure venous blood

steps.x: Mechanism of the delay.
Injury, symptom-free interval, slow decline.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bridging **veins** bleed at low pressure, so blood accumulates **slowly**.

elim: Causes postural headache, not a subdural.
Does not explain a slowly growing collection.

steps.x: **E. Slow accumulation of low-pressure venous blood.** Venous bleed = slow, delayed presentation.

practice.stem: A 79 year old man is brought in by his wife, who says he has been 'acting differently' for 10 days. He has been sleepy, irritable and briefly confused, then normal again. He has atrial fibrillation and has had several falls. His pulse rate is 84 bpm irregularly irregular, BP 150/88 mmHg and temperature 36.8°C.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fluctuating confusion with falls and AF (likely anticoagulated) in an older man is a classic subdural haemorrhage.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an elderly patient with behaviour change.
Fluctuating behaviour and consciousness, AF (likely anticoagulated), falls.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Subdural haemorrhage.**

elim: Possible, but less linked to falls and anticoagulation.
Lucid interval then rapid deterioration after trauma.
Insidious over years, no fluctuating consciousness.

steps.x: **E. Subdural haemorrhage.** Falls + anticoagulation + fluctuation = subdural.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man is hit on the side of the head by a cricket ball. He is briefly knocked out, recovers and talks normally for 2 hours, then rapidly becomes drowsy. His pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 184/96 mmHg. CT head shows a hyperdense crescent-shaped collection over the right hemisphere crossing the coronal suture.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A hyperdense crescent that crosses suture lines is an acute subdural, even with a lucid interval; extradurals are biconvex and stop at sutures.

steps.x: Diagnosis: trust the CT over the story.
The CT decides: bright crescent crossing a suture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bright crescent crossing sutures = **acute subdural**.

elim: The story fits, but extradurals are lens-shaped and stop at sutures.
Blood would lie in cisterns and sulci.

steps.x: **A. Acute subdural haemorrhage.** Crescent + crosses sutures = subdural; hyperdense = acute.

practice.stem: An 83 year old woman on warfarin has had gradually increasing confusion and headache over 3 weeks after a fall. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/82 mmHg. Her GCS is 14.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on CT head?
o: Biconvex hyperdense collection limited by sutures
practice.e: A chronic subdural (over 2 to 3 weeks) is a hypodense crescent crossing suture lines.

steps.x: Most likely CT finding.
Anticoagulated, fall 3 weeks ago, slow decline: chronic subdural.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic subdural = **crescent, hypodense, crosses sutures**.
**C. Crescent-shaped hypodense collection crossing sutures.** Chronic subdural = dark crescent.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man with alcohol dependence is found at home drowsy and confused. Neighbours say he has fallen several times in the past month. His temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. His GCS fluctuates between 11 and 14. He has a left hemiparesis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Alcohol causes atrophy and falls; fluctuating GCS with a focal deficit makes a subdural the best answer.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a confused drinker.
Alcohol (atrophy), falls, fluctuating GCS, focal sign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Subdural haemorrhage.**

elim: Tremor, sweating and tachycardia, without focal signs.
Causes confusion and asterixis, not a hemiparesis; ammonia and LFTs are not given.
Sudden onset, not fluctuating GCS over weeks.
Ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and confusion; no hemiparesis.

steps.x: **D. Subdural haemorrhage.** Drinker + falls + fluctuating GCS + focal sign = subdural.

practice.stem: An 88 year old woman fell and hit her head 6 days ago. She is now drowsy. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg. Her GCS is 13. Her CT head shows an extra-axial collection that is the same density as brain, with effacement of the sulci and 6 mm midline shift.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: An isodense extra-axial collection about a week after injury is a subacute subdural; mass effect gives it away.

steps.x: Diagnosis from the CT density.
Fall a week ago; isodense extra-axial collection with mass effect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Isodense = **subacute subdural**.

elim: An infarct is within the brain, not extra-axial.
Hyperdense lens shape in the acute phase.

steps.x: **E. Subacute subdural haemorrhage.** Hyper = acute, iso = subacute, hypo = chronic.

practice.stem: An 80 year old man has a known chronic subdural being managed conservatively. Today he becomes suddenly more drowsy. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 176/94 mmHg. CT head shows a hypodense crescentic collection containing scattered areas of hyperdensity.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
practice.e: Mixed density (bright fresh blood within a dark old collection) is acute-on-chronic subdural, from rebleeding of fragile neomembranes.

steps.x: Explain the CT and the deterioration.

clues: hypodense crescentic collection containing scattered areas of hyperdensity
steps.x: Old dark collection with new bright blood.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fresh blood in an old collection: **acute-on-chronic subdural**.
**B. Acute-on-chronic subdural haemorrhage.** Mixed density crescent = acute-on-chronic.

practice.stem: An 85 year old woman on warfarin fell at home and hit her head. She has no loss of consciousness, no vomiting and no headache. Her GCS is 15. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 140/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: NICE head injury guidance: anticoagulated patients with a head injury need a CT head within 8 hours even when well, to exclude a subdural.

steps.x: Investigation after head injury in an anticoagulated patient.
Well, but anticoagulated after a head injury.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT head within 8 hours** (NICE head injury guidance).
**A. CT head within 8 hours.** Head injury on anticoagulant = CT within 8 h.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has a non-contrast CT head for fluctuating confusion 4 weeks after a fall. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 150/84 mmHg. The radiologist confirms a subdural haemorrhage.
practice.q: Which is the most likely appearance of the collection?
practice.e: A subdural older than 2 to 3 weeks is a hypodense crescent as the blood liquefies.

steps.x: CT appearance by age.
Subdural, 4 weeks old.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Over 2 to 3 weeks = **hypodense crescent**.
**C. Crescentic and hypodense.** Age of bleed sets the density.

practice.stem: An 82 year old man has a symptomatic chronic subdural haemorrhage with 7 mm midline shift and increasing confusion. His INR has been corrected with IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 150/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Symptomatic chronic subdurals are drained through a burr hole after anticoagulation reversal; craniotomy is for acute clot.

steps.x: Definitive treatment.
Chronic, symptomatic, mass effect, reversal done.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Burr hole craniostomy.**

elim: For large acute subdurals with refractory ICP.

steps.x: **A. Burr hole craniostomy.** Chronic = burr hole.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman taking warfarin for a metallic heart valve has a symptomatic acute subdural haemorrhage on CT. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 170/92 mmHg. Her GCS is 13.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management of her anticoagulation?
o: IV vitamin K 5 mg and 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
practice.e: Intracranial bleeding on warfarin is reversed with IV vitamin K and 4-factor PCC; the bleed outweighs the valve thrombosis risk short term.

steps.x: Reversal agent.
Life-threatening bleed on warfarin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV vitamin K 5 mg + 4-factor PCC**, even with a metal valve.

elim: Slower and less effective than PCC.
Far too slow for an intracranial bleed.

steps.x: **C. IV vitamin K 5 mg and 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate.** Warfarin bleed = vitamin K + PCC.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has a small acute subdural haemorrhage after a fall. He is not anticoagulated. His GCS is 15 and he has no focal signs. CT shows a thin collection with no midline shift. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 142/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Observation with neurological checks and serial CT
practice.e: Small asymptomatic acute subdurals are observed with regular examination and serial CT; surgery is for shift >5 mm, raised ICP or deterioration.

steps.x: Management of a small bleed.
Small, asymptomatic acute bleed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Observe** with regular neuro checks and **serial CT**.

elim: Needs raised ICP, shift >5 mm or deterioration.

steps.x: **E. Observation with neurological checks and serial CT.** Small and well = observe.

practice.stem: An 86 year old man with marked cerebral atrophy on a previous scan develops a subdural haemorrhage after a minor bump on a cupboard door. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 138/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which best explains why a trivial injury caused bleeding?
o: Atrophy stretches bridging veins, making them vulnerable to shearing
Fracture of the temporal bone tearing the middle meningeal artery
practice.e: Brain atrophy widens the gap that bridging veins must cross, stretching them so minor shearing forces tear them.

steps.x: Mechanism.
Atrophy plus trivial trauma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Atrophy **stretches bridging veins**, so minor shear tears them.
**A. Atrophy stretches bridging veins, making them vulnerable to shearing.** Atrophy + bridging veins = subdural after trivial trauma.
